teach.title: What it does
teach.say: The 'must be done' pattern usually names the person who must do it, and that person goes in the dative (the 'to/for' form). That is **the dative of agent (the person who must do it: mihi legendum est = I must read)**. *Hic liber mihi legendus est* is word for word 'this book is to-be-read for me', and in plain English 'I have to read this book'.

check.ask: What is tibi doing beside tacendum est?

teach.title: The pronouns: mihi, tibi, nōbīs, vōbīs
teach.say: The commonest doers are the pronouns: *mihi* I, *tibi* you, *nōbīs* we, *vōbīs* you (more than one). *mihi* and *nōbīs* are the dative singular and plural of *ego*, printed below; *tū* makes *tibi* and *vōbīs* the same way. They are the very forms you already use for 'give it to me'.

check.ask: Fill in the form of ego that means 'we have to'.

teach.title: Nouns take their ordinary dative endings
teach.say: A named person or a whole group takes the dative its own declension (its own family of endings) gives it: *servō* from *servus* for one slave, *servīs* for all of them together. Nothing special is added for this job — it is the plain dative doing a new one.

check.ask: Fill in the dative plural of servus.

teach.title: Not ā or ab with the ablative
teach.say: An ordinary passive verb names its doer with *ā/ab* and the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form): *liber ā Mārcō legitur*. The gerundive refuses that and takes the bare dative instead: *liber mihi legendus est*. Do not write *ā mē legendus est*.

check.ask: Two doers stand here. What is mihi doing?

teach.title: Not the plain 'to / for' dative
teach.say: The same word can do either job. After a verb of giving, *fīliō* is the person given to: *pater fīliō librum dat*. Beside a gerundive with *sum*, *fīliō* is the person who must act: *fīliō legendus est*, his son has to read it. The gerundive is what changes the job.

check.ask: mihi is the person the book is sent to. What is tibi doing?

teach.title: Use it
teach.say: Name the doer in the dative, match the gerundive to the thing, and add *sum*: *quid nōbīs faciendum est?* — what do we have to do? Where there is no thing at all, the neuter serves: *omnibus puerīs tacendum est*.

check.ask: Fill in the dative of servus that names who had to finish the work.

core.text: With the gerundive + *sum* (the 'must be done' pattern), the person who has to do the job is not *ā* + ablative but **the dative of agent (the person who must do it: mihi legendum est = I must read)**: *liber mihi legendus est* — the book is for me to read, so: I must read the book; *servō faciendum est* — the slave must do it. The dative (the 'to/for' form) fits because the duty is 'for' that person. Latin name: *datīvus auctōris*.
English turns it round: *the book must be read by me* becomes *I must read the book*. Find the dative, make it the subject, say 'must'.
Gerundive + sum + dative = 'X must …': the dative names the doer. ā/ab + ablative is not used with the gerundive.

With an ordinary passive the doer is ā/ab + the ablative (the 'by' form after a/ab): *liber ā puerō legitur* — the book is read by the boy. Only with the gerundive does the doer become dative: *liber puerō legendus est*. So: *-tur / -tus est* → ā + ablative; *-ndus est* → dative.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: some verbs take a dative object anyway (*fīdere* trust, *pārēre* obey). In *amīcīs fīdendum nōn est* (Week 11) *amīcīs* is the ones not to be trusted, not the person who must act. Ask: is the dative the doer, or the verb's own object?

In the course texts only one sentence spells the doer out (*servō faciendum est*, Week 9); the usual case has no doer named — *merum bibendum est*, *tacendum est* (Week 9) — the duty is stated, the person understood. Add one and it goes in the dative: *nōbīs merum bibendum est*.

Ørberg's chapter 31 states the rule in Latin: the person by whom something ought to be done is marked with the gerundive by the dative — *discipulus industrius magistrō laudandus est* (= *ā magistrō*), *Lingua Latīna vōbīs discenda est*, *quidquid magister imperāvit discipulō faciendum est*. The learner's notes for Week 31 describe the participle and *sum* but do not treat the agent; this lesson fills that gap. Allen & Greenough add two edges: when the gerundive verb itself takes a dative (like *fīdere*) or two datives would be confusing, writers fall back on ā/ab + ablative for the doer; and poets sometimes use a dative of agent with a perfect participle too (*mihi cōnsultum est*, care has been taken by me).
